Do LLMs Recognize Your Preferences? Evaluating Personalized Preference Following in LLMs

PrefEval plants a single user preference at the start of a multi-session conversation and asks, turns and tokens later, whether the model's response still honors it. Zero-shot accuracy falls under 20% within ten turns for nine of the ten benchmarked models — o1-preview is the outlier, at 50% — and those nine keep sliding toward the single digits as the conversation stretches to 100k tokens; Reminder prompting and retrieval slow that decay for most models but don't reverse it.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

"Personalization" in most LLM benchmarks means retrieval: tell the model a fact, ask for it back later, see if it survives a long context window. LaMP conditions on a user's writing history to score short-form generation; the "needle-in-a-haystack" family (LongBench, ∞Bench, L-Eval, BABILong) tests whether a fact planted deep in a document can be found again. None of these test whether a model proactively applies what it was told when the topic comes back around — they either hand the model the relevant context right before the question, or they only check whether the fact can be recited, not whether it changes the model's behavior downstream.

PrefEval targets that gap directly: a user states a preference once — "I dislike eating seafood due to an allergy" — and the benchmark measures whether an unrelated later query ("what Japanese dishes should I try?") produces a response that actually respects it, after the preference has been buried under anywhere from a few to hundreds of turns of unrelated multi-session chat pulled from real LMSYS-Chat-1M conversations. The benchmark is deliberately about the kind of preference a chatbot would need to retain over an ongoing relationship with a user — dietary restrictions, travel style, media taste — spanning 20 everyday topics across seven domains (Entertainment, Travel, Lifestyle, Shopping, Education, Pets, and Profession), not one-off task instructions of the kind IFEval or InstructGPT-style instruction-following benchmarks check.

The paper frames this as a distinct axis from long-context QA: it isn't enough for the model to locate the preference statement in the transcript (a retrieval problem); it has to recognize that a much later, topically-unrelated query is the moment to apply it (an inference-and-proactivity problem), across three preference forms of increasing subtlety — stated outright, implied by a two-turn choice, or buried in a 4–8 turn persona-driven dialogue where the preference is never the point of the conversation.

// how it works

The method

PrefEval comprises 3,000 manually curated preference–query pairs spanning 20 topics across seven domains. Each pair is constructed in one of three forms of increasing difficulty: (1) Explicit Preference — a single direct sentence ("I dislike eating seafood due to an allergy"); (2) Implicit Choice-Based — a two-turn exchange where the assistant offers several options, some violating the preference, and the user accepts or rejects one, revealing the preference only through the choice; (3) Implicit Persona-Driven — a 4–8 turn conversation built around an assigned persona, where the preference is mentioned once in passing and is never the conversation's actual topic. To simulate a real ongoing chat rather than an isolated two-turn probe, the authors interleave real multi-session conversation turns sampled from LMSYS-Chat-1M between the preference disclosure and the final query, stretching the gap up to 100k tokens.

Each preference–query pair supports two task types. In the generation task, the model produces a free-form response, which is scored by an "LLM-as-a-judge" pipeline: four independent Claude 3 Sonnet evaluators each answer a binary question about the response (does it violate the preference? acknowledge it? hallucinate a preference that wasn't stated? fail to be helpful?), and these four binary checks are aggregated by a fixed rule table (the paper's Table 1) into one of four disjoint error types — Preference-Unaware Violation, Preference Hallucination Violation, Inconsistency Violation, or Unhelpful Response. "Preference-following accuracy" is defined as the fraction of responses with none of these four errors. In the classification task, the query is instead posed as a multiple-choice question with one preference-aligned option among several violating ones, scored by ordinary accuracy — a cheaper, exact-match proxy the paper validates by showing it correlates with generation-task accuracy (Pearson r = 0.73 across 6 models, 5 methods, and 12 dialogue lengths, each point averaged over 20 topics).

Ten models are benchmarked in total (Table 3): Claude 3 Sonnet, Claude 3 Haiku, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Mistral 7B Instruct, Mixtral 8x7B Instruct, LLaMA 3 8B Instruct, LLaMA 3 70B Instruct, GPT-4o, o1-preview, and Gemini-1.5-Pro. Four intervention methods are compared on top of the raw zero-shot baseline (five conditions in total): a one-sentence Reminder appended before the model answers; Self-Critic (generate, critique against the preference, then revise); a Few-Shot Chain-of-Thought demonstration of preference-aware reasoning; and Retrieval-Augmented Generation, which embeds conversation turns with a sentence-transformer and retrieves the top-k (k=5, chosen after an ablation in Fig. 12 comparing k=5 and k=10) most similar exchanges as context.

To validate the LLM-based grader itself, the authors ran two separate human-agreement checks: a 200-sample spot check reported in the main text ("we manually checked 200 randomly sampled evaluations, with an observed 5% error rate"), and a larger, per-form breakdown in Appendix A.17 — 100 randomly sampled evaluations from each of the three preference forms (300 total), each compared against human annotators' judgments on the same four binary checks plus the aggregated accuracy call (Table 18, discussed under "does it hold up?" below).

// what they found

The results

The headline pattern is a steep, near-universal decay curve. Averaged across 20 topics and six core models (Claude 3 Sonnet, Claude 3 Haiku, Mixtral 8x7B, Mistral 7B, LLaMA3 70B, LLaMA3 8B), zero-shot explicit-preference accuracy starts around 80% at the shortest gap tested (0.2k tokens / a handful of turns) and drops below 30% by merely 5 turns, continuing toward near-zero by 300 turns / ~103k tokens (Figure 3). Breaking this down by the three preference forms and by prompting method (Figure 4, Figure 5) shows the same shape holds for every model, and implicit preferences are generally harder than explicit ones through the short-and-mid-range lengths (0.2k–54k tokens): at 3k tokens / 10 turns, zero-shot explicit accuracy across the six models ranges 10–17%, while zero-shot accuracy on the implicit choice-based form at the same length is already 6–8% for all six. That gap narrows and occasionally reverses at the longest lengths, where all three forms have decayed toward a shared floor — at 84k–103k tokens zero-shot, Claude 3 Haiku is actually slightly higher on the implicit persona-driven form (7%, 8%) than on explicit (6%, 7%).

On the narrower "travel restaurant" slice used to compare the four newest proprietary models (Table 2/Table 4: Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Gemini-1.5-Pro, o1-preview, and — in the appendix version — GPT-4o), the pattern repeats even for frontier models: at 10 turns / ~3k tokens zero-shot, Claude-3.5-Sonnet and Gemini-1.5-Pro both score 0.07 and GPT-4o scores 0.07, while o1-preview alone reaches 0.50 (a result the paper itself flags as possibly unfair, since o1-preview's extra test-time "thinking" phase is not available to the other models). Reminder recovers most models into the 0.9s at 10 turns, but by 300 turns / ~103k tokens even Reminder is down to 0.02–0.23 for three of the four models — only o1-preview holds at 0.98.

Two secondary findings run against naive intuition. First, more stated preferences within a conversation improve, rather than hurt, adherence to the first one — preference-following accuracy for the earliest-stated preference rises monotonically from roughly 0.32 (at 2 total preferences stated) to roughly 0.47 (at 20), as more later, unrelated preferences are inserted after it (Figure 8). A related but distinct experiment finds a similar reinforcing effect running the other direction in time: when a second preference on the same topic is stated earlier in the conversation, before the original preference that is actually queried (and stated later), adherence to that later original preference improves — a single stated preference gives a baseline accuracy near 0.20 for both Claude 3 Haiku and Claude 3 Sonnet, but an earlier conflicting preference raises this to roughly 0.40–0.44 and an earlier non-conflicting preference to roughly 0.31 (Figure 9) — the authors attribute the boost to a "topic-reinforcement effect," where even a contradicting restatement keeps the topic (e.g., response length, dietary restriction) salient. Second, supervised fine-tuning on PrefEval itself substantially closes the gap: fine-tuning Mistral-7B on 80% of PrefEval's topics (using its own Reminder-method responses at 0, 5, and 10 inserted contextual turns) and testing on the held-out 20% of topics improves zero-shot accuracy and — notably — generalizes to context lengths longer than anything seen in training. The paper further shows this generalizes to the implicit forms the model was never fine-tuned on (Table 17): on the Travel Restaurants topic, implicit persona-driven accuracy jumps from 1.79% to 55.36% after SFT, and implicit choice-based from 3.57% to 14.29%; on Travel Hotels, persona-driven goes from 14.81% to 74.07% and choice-based from 11.11% to 51.85% — in both topics the persona-driven gain (+53.6pp, +59.3pp) is larger than the choice-based gain (+10.7pp, +40.7pp), consistent with the paper's claim that fine-tuning "brings more improvements for Implicit Persona-Driven preferences."

Error-type analysis (Figure 13, Appendix A.10) shows the failure mode shifting with the intervention: under Zero-Shot, the dominant error by far is Preference-Unaware Violation — the model simply doesn't bring the preference to bear at all, with counts plateauing near 900 in that panel, though only two of the six core models are actually tracked out to turn 150 (Claude 3 Sonnet and Claude 3 Haiku); the Llama3 series stop at their context limit around turn 10 and the Mistral series around turn 70. Once a prompting method reminds the model to consider the preference (Reminder, CoT, Self-Critic, RAG), Preference-Unaware Violation drops but Preference Hallucination Violation and Unhelpful Response both rise sharply instead, and it's the two Claude models that account for most of it — Claude 3 Sonnet racks up hundreds of Unhelpful-Response errors under CoT and Self-Critic (consistent with the paper's own narrower observation, from a two-model comparison in Figure 7, that Sonnet often refuses to answer when it perceives insufficient context about the user's preference), while Claude 3 Haiku shows the same pattern instead under Reminder and RAG. In other words, the prompting methods that reduce outright preference-blindness trade it for a different failure — hallucinating a preference that was never stated, or declining to give a substantive answer at all.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

PrefEval's grading pipeline is unusually well-instrumented for a paper that relies on an LLM judge. Table 18 reports per-checker human–LLM agreement, computed by sampling 100 evaluations from each of the three preference forms (300 total) and comparing human annotators' judgments against Claude 3 Sonnet's on all four binary checks plus the final aggregated accuracy call. Agreement ranges from 0.86 (Violate-Preference check, Implicit Choice-based) to 0.98 (Hallucinate-Preference check, Explicit); on the final Preference-Following-Accuracy call specifically, agreement is 0.97 / 0.92 / 0.96 for Explicit / Implicit-Choice / Implicit-Persona respectively — a mean of 0.95, which lines up closely with the separate 200-sample check reported in the main text ("an observed 5% error rate"). That's a genuinely validated LLM grader in its own setting, not a grader the paper merely asserts is reliable — worth crediting explicitly, since papers proposing an LLM-based metric routinely skip this step. But the validation's own provenance is thin: neither §2.5 ("we manually checked") nor Appendix A.17 ("human annotators") ever says how many raters there were, who they were, how they were recruited or qualified, or whether any inter-annotator agreement was computed — a 0.95-mean agreement figure whose human side could be one person or several, and could include the authors themselves, is weaker evidence than the confident framing implies. The lowest cell (0.86, on whether a response violates an implicitly-revealed choice-based preference) is also worth flagging: it's the one place the grader itself is weakest, and at 3k tokens, in the zero-shot rows, it coincides with the hardest of the three preference forms in the benchmark's own results — averaged across the six core models, choice-based is the lowest of the three at that length — though the paper is explicit that which implicit form is harder is model-dependent at other lengths ("Claude and Llama struggle more with implicit persona-driven preferences... while Mistral models show the opposite trend," §3.3), so this alignment shouldn't be read as a general pattern.

The more structural question is how much of the "preference-following" decay is really about preferences at all, versus ordinary long-context degradation that would show up on any planted-fact-retrieval task. The paper's own Appendix A.15 investigation (Figure 23) is the right control here, and it's informative: inserting the same preference at different locations within a fixed 100-turn conversation (Claude 3 Sonnet and Claude 3 Haiku, four topics) shows accuracy dipping specifically when the preference sits mid-conversation (around turn 50) relative to the beginning or end — the paper explicitly connects this to Liu et al.'s "Lost in the Middle" finding about positional degradation in long-context retrieval. That is a genuine, useful disentanglement: it shows position, not just raw distance, drives part of the failure, which means at least some of PrefEval's difficulty is inherited from a known long-context weakness rather than being specific to preference-following per se. But the paper doesn't go the further step of directly comparing preference-following decay against a matched fact-retrieval task (e.g., a "needle" that isn't a preference) at the same lengths and positions, so a reader can't cleanly separate "how much worse is preference application than fact recall" from these results alone — the U-shaped curve confirms long-context effects are present, not how large a share of the headline collapse they explain.

The mechanistic story in Section 3.7 (SFT improves attention to the preference region) is real but modest, and worth reading at the scale it was measured. Across 100 held-out test examples, fine-tuning increases the fraction of generation-time attention mass falling on the preference-statement tokens by a mean of 2.50 percentage points (median 2.58, min 0.51, max 4.97) — every one of the 100 examples shows a positive shift, which is a clean, consistent direction of effect, but it is a small one, measured only on Mistral-7B, and it is correlational: an increase in attention mass co-occurring with improved accuracy after SFT is consistent with the paper's causal story but doesn't establish it (the fine-tuned model differs from the base model in every one of its weights, not just where it looks).

On construct validity: every preference and every query in PrefEval is LLM-generated (Claude 3.5 Sonnet was used to draft personas and persona-driven conversations, per Appendix A.13) and then manually filtered, rather than drawn from real user transcripts. The preferences in the scored 3,000-pair benchmark are static for the whole conversation — stated once and never revised, which is why PersonaMem's own comparison table records PrefEval, like LOCOMO, as "No update" (LongMemEval is credited with 1 knowledge update, PersonaMem with 3). The paper does probe revision separately, in §3.6's auxiliary five-topic conflicting-preference study (Figure 9) — but that's a small side analysis outside the scored benchmark, not a systematic account of preferences changing over the course of a conversation, which real personalization also has to handle. A second scope note: the paper's Appendix A.1 (Limitation) is upfront that the benchmark evaluates preference-following, not the factual correctness of what's recommended, and separately notes the implicit-choice construction doesn't guarantee the user's single accepted option perfectly isolates the preference — though the authors only say that, given how high the strongest baseline scores in early turns (around 90%), they "believe the errors should be within an acceptable range," without giving a specific error-rate estimate.

One internal inconsistency worth flagging plainly rather than smoothing over: the text immediately preceding Table 4 states "We did not evaluate GPT-4o with 300 turns due to budget limit," yet Table 4 itself prints GPT-4o values for both 300-turn columns (Zero-shot 0.05, Reminder 0.23). One of these two statements in the paper is wrong; a reader relying on Table 4's GPT-4o/300-turn cells should treat the "not evaluated" sentence as the likelier stale artifact (the numbers are internally consistent with the rest of the table's structure), but the paper as published does not resolve which is correct.

baselines

Ten models spanning three vendors plus two open-weight families, evaluated across five conditions (a Zero-Shot baseline plus four interventions: Reminder, Self-Critic, CoT, RAG). Fair and current for a Feb-2025 submission; o1-preview's inclusion is honestly caveated by the authors as possibly unfair given its extra test-time compute.

contamination

Preferences and queries are synthetic (LLM-drafted, human-filtered) rather than scraped from public data the models could have memorized, which is a genuine contamination advantage — but it also means the benchmark's preferences may not match how real users actually phrase preferences "in the wild," a construct-validity tradeoff the paper doesn't explicitly discuss.

what's missed

No head-to-head control isolating how much of the decay is preference-specific versus ordinary long-context retrieval difficulty at matched positions; the scored 3,000-pair benchmark keeps preferences static for the whole conversation (§3.6's revision probe is a small 5-topic side analysis, not part of the scored set); the SFT attention-mechanism evidence is real but small (mean +2.5pp) and shown on one model only.

would raise confidence

A matched non-preference "needle" control at identical turn/token positions; the same human-agreement study run on a second LLM judge besides Claude 3 Sonnet; disclosing the Table 18 study's human-annotator count, qualifications, and any inter-annotator agreement; resolving the Table 4 / prose GPT-4o-300-turn discrepancy; extending the SFT attention analysis to a second base model.

// bottom line

PrefEval is a carefully built, unusually well human-validated benchmark for a real and under-tested capability — proactively applying a preference stated once, long ago, in an unrelated conversation. The headline finding (accuracy collapsing within a handful of turns, without explicit prompting, across nine of the ten benchmarked models — o1-preview is the one exception) is well-supported and the grader is genuinely validated against humans rather than merely asserted, though the human side of that validation is itself under-documented (see below). The open question the paper leaves for future work is how much of that collapse is preference-following specifically versus the long-context degradation any planted fact would suffer at the same position — the paper gestures at this with its Lost-in-the-Middle control but stops short of a matched comparison that would pin down the split.

// what to remember

What to remember

  1. PrefEval tests whether a stated preference is proactively applied to a later, topically-unrelated query — not whether it can merely be retrieved — across 3,000 pairs, 20 topics, and three preference forms of increasing subtlety (explicit, implicit choice-based, implicit persona-driven).
  2. Without prompting, preference-following accuracy for the six core models falls from roughly 80% to under 30% by just 5 turns and keeps decaying toward zero by 300 turns / ~100k tokens; the four frontier models (Table 2/4) show the same collapse, with o1-preview the only one that starts high unprompted — alone near 50% at 10 turns — and it gives most of that back, falling to 14% by 300 turns while the other three simply sit on the floor throughout (0.07 → 0.02–0.09). Reminder prompting and RAG slow the decay for most models without stopping it, and the failure mode shifts from "ignoring the preference outright" (Zero-Shot) to hallucinating one or refusing to answer (once a prompting method is applied).
  3. The LLM-based grader (Claude 3 Sonnet) is genuinely validated against human judgment — 300 sampled evaluations across the three preference forms give 0.86–0.98 per-checker agreement, consistent with a separate 200-sample, 5%-error-rate check in the main text — which is a real methodological strength, not just an assertion.
